newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian party plays down signs of alliance.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian party plays down signs of alliance.

text.p: Tens of thousands of supporters of Indonesia's Moslem-based party campaigned in Jakarta on Wednesday for the coming election, but signs of an alliance with the ousted leader of a rival party were muted, witnesses said.
The government has banned slogans, banners and pictures linking the ousted leader of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), Megawati Sukarnoputri, to the Moslem-based United Development Party (PPP).

The PPP and the PDI are battling the much-larger ruling party, Golkar, for 425 seats in parliament at general elections set for May 29. Another 75 seats in the house are allotted to appointees from the military, which does not vote.

Despite the ban, pictures of Megawati, the charismatic daughter of the late founding president Sukarno, were seen being carried by supporters. But they were less in evidence than at previous PPP rallies.
Also muted were displays of flags and banners proclaiming a "Mega-Bintang" alliance. The bintang, or star, is the PPP symbol.
Witnesses said police also appeared to be strictly enforcing traffic regulations when the PPP took out illegal convoys of vehicles after campaign rallies, but there was no violence.
Megawati was ousted from the PDI leadership last year by a government-backed faction headed by deputy parliament speaker Surjadi and has been barred from participating in the elections.
She had asked her supporters to boycott the election campaign, but appears to have tacitly approved their alliance with the PPP as a way to register disapproval of the other PDI faction.
Although political analysts have said the link-up will have little or no effect on Golkar's forecast easy win, there have been signs that ruling circles are worried.
Abdul Gafur, the most senior of Golkar's seven chairmen, said his party supported the ban.

"Every slogan and every theme should be approved by the police, and this one is not permitted as it has not been given permission by the police," Gafur, second in the party's rankings after general chairman Harmoko, told Reuters in an interview.
"The government only recognises one PDI led by Surjadi," said Gafur, a former minister. The involvement of police in the regulation of campaign slogans was not anti-democratic, he said.

"If the government does not set up rules like that sometimes they will make anti-government and anti-religion slogans that could be very dangerous. We just want to uphold something that is very important, that is, the unity of the nation," he said.

Attorney-General Singgih, head of the official election supervision committee, was quoted as saying on Tuesday that President Suharto had ordered him to enforce the new rules, which prohibit banners and pictures linking Megawati and PPP.
"We ask the three contestants' task forces to haul down those banners and pictures," Singgih said, adding that banners and other campaign material must be approved by the police.

Golkar, in power for the last 30 years under Suharto, is seeking to push its share of the vote to more than 70 percent from the 68 percent it won at the last polls in 1992. The PPP won 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent.
